indicators.note: return asks for the teachers' union abbreviation to be read backwards

parts.note: the NUT was the National Union of Teachers in Britain
taken as written

explanation.surface: Teachers coming back to work are the city's main asset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns NUT into TUN, then IS follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunis is the capital city of Tunisia.

parts.note: a test is a trial run, done for practice
to strike a match is to light it, and a match is struck

explanation.surface: A worldwide walkout staged as a rehearsal.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket and rugby an 'international' is a match between national teams.
explanation.definitionFit: A test match is a game between national sides, chiefly in cricket.

clue.text: French city incomplete? By no means!

indicators.note: incomplete means the city name is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: Nevers is a city in central France

explanation.surface: Is a French city unfinished? Not at all!
explanation.definitionFit: Never as an exclamation means not on any account, an emphatic refusal.

clue.text: To be honest, that rig's out of order

indicators.note: out of order means the letters are not in their proper sequence

parts.note: the apostrophe is dropped, giving its letters

explanation.surface: Frankly, that equipment is broken.
explanation.definitionFit: Straight means frank, truthful and law-abiding.

parts.note: CA is short for circa, Latin for about
CO is the abbreviation for company
a phony is a fake or impostor

explanation.surface: A dispute concerning a company caught up in a swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' here rhymes with 'cow', a din, not a quarrel; 'involving' just links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A row in the sense of a loud noise is a harsh, discordant racket.

parts.note: C is short for circa, about
lip and sauce both mean cheek, impudence

explanation.surface: A movie excerpt about a condiment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sauce' is not a condiment but cheeky talk, as is LIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A clip is a short extract from a movie.

clue.text: Assemble and leave without great upheaval

indicators.note: without in the old sense of outside, so the word for leave surrounds the rest

parts.note: a conge is formal leave to depart, or a dismissal

indicators.note: an upheaval is a violent disturbance, so the letters of great are churned

explanation.surface: Gather and depart without any great fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside here; 'upheaval' turns GREAT into REGAT, which sits inside CONGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To congregate is to gather together in a crowd.

explanation.surface: A pill for toothache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tablet' suggests a pill but means a flat inscribed slab.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaque is a commemorative slab; dental plaque is the film on teeth that causes decay.

clue.text: Stirring love song doesn't start, nor does love

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

indicators.note: doesn't start means the opening letter of the word for song is dropped

parts.note: an anthem is a song

indicators.note: nor does means the second love also loses its opening letter

explanation.surface: A moving love song that never starts, nor does the romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doesn't start' takes A from ANTHEM, leaving NTHEM, and 'nor does' takes L from LOVE, leaving OVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Stirring here means moving about, in motion and busy.

clue.text: Boat turning up in the island out east

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up reads the whole run backwards, bottom to top
out means the compass letter is removed from the

parts.note: a cay is a small low island

explanation.surface: A vessel showing up at an island in the far east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes E from THE leaving TH; TH plus CAY gives THCAY, and 'turning up' turns that whole run round.
explanation.definitionFit: A yacht is a sailing or motor vessel used for pleasure or racing.

clue.text: Mark, comprising unused note or coin

indicators.note: comprising means the word for mark holds the other pieces within it

parts.note: a sign is a mark or symbol
something left over is unused
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: A hallmark on a fresh banknote or a coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A sovereign is a British gold coin once worth one pound.

explanation.surface: A Greek tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Attic describes things of ancient Athens; an attic is the top storey of a house, and story is the American spelling of storey.

explanation.surface: A bird that can work magic.
explanation.definitionFit: The merlin is a small falcon; Merlin is the wizard of Arthurian legend, a man with magical powers.

clue.text: The reasons advanced are not about to stick

indicators.note: about means the contraction for are not goes round the word for stick

parts.note: aren't is the contraction of are not
to gum is to stick or glue

explanation.surface: Excuses offered that will not hold together.
explanation.definitionFit: An argument is a case or line of reasoning put forward to persuade.

explanation.surface: Similar to creeping on hands and knees.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes cases exactly comparable; it also describes moving on hands and knees.

clue.text: Hairy Hugo can't do with dishevelment

indicators.note: dishevelment is untidiness, so the letters of the three words are messed up

parts.note: the apostrophe is dropped, giving its letters

explanation.surface: Hugo, with his shaggy hair, cannot cope with being untidy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hairy' looks like a description of Hugo; it is the definition, slang for risky.
explanation.definitionFit: Hairy is informal for dangerous or uncertain, and a touch-and-go situation is precarious with the outcome in doubt.

explanation.surface: A mad place for a flag.
explanation.walkthrough: British slang 'up the pole' means mad; a flag literally flies at the top of its pole.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for mad or mistaken; a raised flag sits at the top of its mast.

explanation.surface: Looking for honey.
explanation.definitionFit: To comb is to search thoroughly; bees store honey in a comb of wax cells.

explanation.surface: A dabbler as a swimmer.
explanation.definitionFit: A flighty, superficial person is a social butterfly; the butterfly is also a swimming style.

clue.text: Welsh engineers first to supply material

indicators.note: first places the engineers ahead of the other piece

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
to welsh is to run off without paying a debt, which is also to levant

explanation.surface: Welsh engineers are the first to supply materials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welsh' is not about Wales: to welsh (or levant) is to abscond without paying a bet.
explanation.definitionFit: Material in the legal sense means pertinent, bearing on the matter in hand.

indicators.note: displays says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: The feeling a foe shows.
explanation.definitionFit: Hatred, intense dislike, is a strong feeling.

explanation.surface: The top-ranked players need fortune on their side.
explanation.walkthrough: Seeded players in a tournament are its strongest entrants; 'need' only links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Seeds are the top-ranked competitors; the phrase is also a farewell wish for success.

clue.text: Figure socially acceptable in Washington, for instance

indicators.note: in means the letter for socially acceptable goes inside the other word

parts.note: Washington is one US state
U means upper-class, socially acceptable, in British usage

explanation.surface: A personality respected in the US capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Washington' points to the state, not the city; U is the old British label for upper-class usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A statue is a sculpted human form, a carved figure.

indicators.note: I say marks the pieces as heard spoken rather than written

parts.note: to die away is to fade; hard cheese is British slang for tough luck, so tough

explanation.surface: Someone sympathises sarcastically when the colour washes out of their clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard cheese!' is British slang for 'bad luck!', here giving TOUGH; DIES plus TOUGH spoken give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dyestuff is a substance used to give cloth its tint.

parts.note: reads as a day of the week but refers to the author of the novel featuring Man Friday, the castaway's servant

explanation.surface: A writer at work at the end of the week.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel Defoe wrote Robinson Crusoe, in which Friday is the hero's companion.

clue.text: Turned into an insect, round river

indicators.note: round means the insect's letters go around the river's

parts.note: a bee is an insect
the Cam is the river flowing through Cambridge

explanation.surface: Metamorphosed into a bug beside a stream.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Kafka-like transformation; 'Turned into' is just the past tense of become.
explanation.definitionFit: If one thing turned into another, it grew to be that thing.

explanation.surface: An animal spotted in the warm season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'summer' reads as the season but is one who sums, a calculator.
explanation.definitionFit: The adder is a venomous snake; a summer, one who adds up, also fits.

indicators.note: out signals the letters of shut are put out of their order

explanation.surface: Closed off, in this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Thus means in this manner or so.

clue.text: Jack finishes off water, to Jill's regret

indicators.note: finishes points to the final letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Jack ends up in the water, which Jill regrets, as in the nursery rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme's Jack and Jill misdirect: 'Jack' is Jack Frost, the personification of wintry weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack Frost is the folk figure personifying icy weather, so Jack stands for it.

clue.text: Found out about judge in novel

indicators.note: about means the jumbled letters go around the word for judge
out signals the letters of found are put out of order

parts.note: to hear a case is to judge it

explanation.surface: Discovered something concerning a judge in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges FOUND into UNDOF, and 'about' puts HEAR inside. 'novel' looks like a book but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Something never known before is new and original.

clue.text: Refreshment for cricketers? Yes, after the start

parts.note: cricket teams are elevens, eleven players a side

indicators.note: after the start means take only what follows the first letter of yes

explanation.surface: Someone agrees that the cricket teams want a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: Elevenses is a British mid-morning snack, taken around 11 o'clock. 'after the start' drops Y from YES.
explanation.definitionFit: A light mid-morning snack with tea or coffee is a bite of food and drink.

explanation.surface: Linger, tacky.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarry is to linger or delay; covered in tar means tacky.
